7467:
You confirm or complete your four-person committee. Some of you arrive with a committee already listed on your Plan of Work, and some arrive without one. Either way, hand in either confirmation from your committee, or a short written plan naming the faculty you will ask, where each conversation stands, and when you expect answers. Either one meets the threshold when it is honest.

  • What you hand in: A forwarded email from your chair, or a one-page plan
  • Due: Before class, Thursday, March 4 (Week 8)
  • Weight: 15% of the final grade
  • Submit: Canvas or email
  • What happens next: Your committee’s responses shape the exam list you submit on March 24

What the program requires

  • Four members, including the chair. A fifth member needs the Director of Graduate Programs’ approval.
  • The chair comes from the CRDM core faculty.
  • At least one member from Communication and one from English. Members from outside NC State need Graduate School approval.
  • A Graduate School Representative joins for the oral preliminary exam. The Graduate School assigns this person, who does not vote. You do not recruit one.
  • Timing: the program asks you to name your advisor and committee by the end of your third semester, on the Plan of Work. If yours has changed since, the Plan of Work needs reapproval.

Why you do it

Your committee reads your exam list, examines you on it, and later reads your dissertation. A list built before you know who those readers are answers to no one in particular. So the committee comes first. This order also gives faculty time: February replies run slow, and a conversation started in Week 6 has a month to develop before your list is due.

Step by step

  1. Week 6 (February 18): draft your committee map and first email. We workshop the email in class with a recently advanced student. Send it within 48 hours.
  2. Weeks 6 and 7: meet your likely chair, or your current chair if you have one. Ask how they work with students, how often they meet, and whom they would suggest for the other seats.
  3. Week 7: ask your remaining members, checking the Communication and English requirement as you go.
  4. By March 4: write up where things stand, as Option A or Option B, and submit before class.
  5. After March 4: keep going. Bring your committee’s responses to the Week 9 canon audit and to your Week 10 meeting, which you book on my calendar.

Full guide, with examples, the self-check table, and assessment levels: https://crd709cole.org/milestones/m2-committee-confirmation.html

7465:
You hand in a working version of the reading list for your comprehensive exam, with one paragraph explaining why the list takes the shape it does. The list develops in stages: ten texts in Week 7, a working draft for peer review in Week 8, a canon audit in Week 9, and the graded version on March 24.

  • What you hand in: A list with full citations, organized into sections, and a one-paragraph rationale
  • Due: By 11:59 pm, Wednesday, March 24
  • Weight: 25% of the final grade
  • Submit: Canvas, email, or a print copy at your Week 10 meeting
  • Models: The folder of past CRDM exam lists

Why you do it

Your comprehensive exam tests whether you know the fields your dissertation answers to. The list defines those fields for you and your committee. It also makes an argument: it says which conversations your project joins, which it sets aside, and where you stand. A list with no argument is a bibliography. A list with one tells your committee what kind of scholar you are becoming. The draft need not be final, but it must be real.

Step by step

  1. Week 7 (February 25): ten texts. Bring ten texts you expect on your list, each tagged with its field and one sentence on why it belongs. Browse the past lists first.
  2. Week 8 (March 4): a working draft for peer review. Bring the list in sections with a draft rationale, plus one past list you admire or would argue with. A partner responds in writing to five prompts listed in the full guide.
  3. Week 9 (March 11): the canon audit. With Haraway in hand, you audit your own draft and two past lists, then make one addition and one cut.
  4. March 11 to 24: revise with your committee. Fold in what your chair and readers say, and bring the list to your Week 10 meeting.
  5. By March 24: submit the graded version.

Full guide, with examples, the self-check table, and assessment levels: https://crd709cole.org/milestones/m3-draft-exam-list.html

7469:
You write a proposal for your dissertation. It argues there is a problem worth investigating, you are positioned to investigate it, and you have a principled method for doing so. You hand it in twice: a complete draft for the Week 14 workshop, and a revised final version during our exam slot.

  • What you hand in: A prospectus with five elements: problem, conversation, method, stakes, and a chapter outline
  • Workshop draft: By 11:59 pm, Wednesday, April 14, with a one-paragraph director’s note. Not graded.
  • Final version: By 11:00 am, Thursday, April 29, our scheduled exam slot
  • Weight: 40% of the final grade
  • Length: No set length. Write what the four elements need.
  • Submit: Canvas, email, print, or a Google Drive link

Why you do it

The prospectus is the document your committee approves before you begin the dissertation. Writing a version now, with a cohort to read it, means you meet your committee with a draft which has already survived questions. It also gathers the semester’s work: the identity statement gives you the stakes, the exam list gives you the conversation, and the Week 11 activity gives you the argument for your method.

Step by step

  1. Week 10: seed writing. Bring 300 to 500 words to your individual meeting: “The problem my dissertation addresses is ___, and it matters because ___.”
  2. Week 11 (March 25): first paragraph and method. Bring a first prospectus paragraph, then argue for your method in class.
  3. Week 12 (April 1): stakes. The “so what” gauntlet presses on why the project matters, and a CRDM graduate talks about where a dissertation goes.
  4. Week 13 (April 8): audiences. Three versions of your project for three readers.
  5. By April 14: the workshop draft. Upload a complete draft with a director’s note.
  6. Week 14 (April 15): workshop. Your group responds with the protocol on the Week 14 page.
  7. Week 15 (April 22): presentation. Five to ten minutes on what you are doing, why it matters, and what you are still working out.
  8. By 11:00 am, April 29: the final version.

Full guide, with examples, the self-check table, and assessment levels: https://crd709cole.org/milestones/m4-prospectus.html
